newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha blames left, vows to end revolt.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha blames left, vows to end revolt.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha has rejected opposition demands for a coalition government and says he is unshaken in his drive to crush the violent unrest in the Balkan state that has killed at least 20 people.
Authorities acknowledged on Tuesday that several southern towns remained out of their control and were in the hands of armed gangs despite the weekend imposition of emergency rule.

In a statement read on state television, Berisha accused leaders of the opposition Socialist Party of resorting to violence and snubbing his bid to restore order, including an offer of early elections.

He rejected their calls for a broad-based government to haul Europe's poorest country out of the crisis triggered by the collapse of dubious pyramid investment schemes into which many Albanians had poured their life savings.

"You decided to overturn the constitutional order and Albanian democracy through an armed rebellion and created a grave problem for the country," Berisha said in the statement, which followed talks with opposition politicians.
"It is not up to me to decide which party or parties are going to make up a coalition. I am against a coalition between the Democratic Party and the Socialist Party."
Western countries which backed Berisha when he came to power in 1992 two years after the collapse of Europe's harshest communist government, criticised the emergency measures.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo, representing the European Union, scheduled a trip to Tirana for Friday. The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe pledged a similar mission.
The U.S. State Department accused Albania of intimidating opposition politicians and trying to shut down the press.
Berisha was elected to a new five-year term on Monday by parliament, where his Democratic Party holds nearly all the seats.
In his statement, Berisha pledged to keep to a minimum the effects of the state of emergency, particularly curbs on press freedoms. These, he said, did not apply at all to foreign media.
International television companies were able to resume broadcasts from Albania on Tuesday less than 24 hours after they were halted by authorities.

But information remained scarce on events in troubled areas of southern Albania, where armed gangs went on the rampage last weekend, ignoring Berisha's concession of dismissing unpopular Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi.

State television said authorities had yet to restore control over the Adriatic port of Vlore where the first outbreak of violence flared last month, pitting police against protesters blaming Berisha for the loss of their savings in the shady investment funds.
Food, it said, was in short supply after a grain depot near the city had been raided.

State television portrayed the situation in the rest of the country as normal. It said commercial aircraft were flying as scheduled into Tirana airport, where reconstruction was proceeding normally, and ports were working without disruption.
It also reported a telegram of congratulations for Berisha on his re-election -- from Ibrahim Rugova, leader of ethnic Albanians in Kosovo, a province of neighbouring Serbia.
The Italian Defence Ministry said on Tuesday an Albanian military plane had landed in southern Italy and that its two pilots had asked for political asylum.
They told Italian authorities they left rather than obey orders to fire on demonstrators in Gjirokaster near the Greek border.
